newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran to choose new president amid vote-rigging fears.
newsitem.headline: Iran to choose new president amid vote-rigging fears.

text.p: Iran votes for a new president on Friday after a fierce campaign in which the Islamic republic's top two officials tried to calm fears of vote-rigging.
Supreme spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and retiring President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani separately warned against any attempt to tamper with ballots and promised the election would be fair.
Four candidates are competing for the presidency which Rafsanjani is bound by law to vacate in August after eight years in office.
But Iranian analysts said only two had any realistic chance of being elected -- left-leaning former cabinet minister Mohammad Khatami and parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri.
Khatami is supported by women, youths and intellectuals and is expected to sweep the capital and some other major cities.
Nateq-Nouri is popular with conservative clergy and Iran's merchant class of bazaaris. He is stronger in rural areas.

Both men are Shi'ite Moslem clerics. They and the other two candidates, Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri and Reza Zavarei, were scrutinised by a body of senior clerics and lawyers for their belief in Iran's Islamic system of government before they were allowed to stand. Some 234 other contenders were rejected.
Iranian analysts and Western diplomats said the election was too close to call.
The presidency is Iran's highest elective office but ranks second to that of the spiritual leader who has absolute power over all state institutions.

More than 33 million Iranians aged 15 and over are eligible to vote in 33,000 polling stations. Three officials will observe the voting at each station and 200,000 police will be on duty to guard against electoral violations.
These include: registering more than one vote, creating an atmosphere of fear or bullying, purchasing votes, and using the identities of children under the age of 15 who are not qualified to vote.
Some 280 people were arrested in Tehran up to Sunday for unspecified violations.
Polling stations are due to open at 8:00 a.m. (0330 GMT) and close at 8:00 p.m. (1530 GMT).
The result is expected to be known by Monday, but if no clear winner emerges with more than 50 percent of the votes the two leading candidates will face a run-off, probably a week later.
